topic: Training-Serving Skew Silently Destroys ML Accuracy
postText:
Your predictive model scores a pristine 98% F1-score in offline validation.
Yet, two weeks into live clinical triage, prediction accuracy silently plummets into chaotic coin tosses.

In healthcare IT, this failure pattern is almost never bad model weights—it is training-serving skew.

At offline training time, data scientists transform patient vitals using batch window aggregations in Pandas. In production, backend engineers re-implement those exact same aggregations in Go or Java over Redis or Kafka streams. Even a microscopic divergence—millisecond timestamp shifts, missing categorical fallbacks, or subtle UTC timezone parsing differences—silently corrupts input feature vectors. The neural network never crashes; it merely serves confident, garbage inferences on live hospital workflows.

We solved this architectural drift by enforcing three production guardrails:
1. Single-Definition Feature Stores: Zero dual-code implementations. Features use identical declarative transformation logic for both offline batch training and online low-latency lookups.
2. Real-Time Distribution Drift Telemetry: Every inference payload runs through continuous Kolmogorov-Smirnov and population stability index (PSI) checks to catch vector drift before outputs hit end-users.
3. Shadow Dual-Inference Pipelines: Candidate ML pipelines run parallel to baseline models on live traffic, comparing outputs asynchronously without impacting P99 latency.

Have you ever caught silent training-serving skew corrupting your production models before users did? What telemetry caught it?
